title: Plato's Theory of Forms
subtitle: Why no circle you have ever drawn is truly a circle
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain the difference between Forms and particulars, and why Plato thought Forms must exist.
By the end you will be able to describe the 'two worlds' picture and how it combines insights from Heraclitus and Parmenides.
By the end you will be able to retell the slave-boy episode in the *Meno* and explain the theory of recollection.
By the end you will be able to state the Third Man objection and explain why it troubled Plato himself.
hook:
Take a pencil and draw a circle. However careful you are, it is not perfect. Zoom in with a microscope and the line wobbles; it has thickness; some points are slightly farther from the center than others. Every circle you have ever seen, on a coin, a wheel or a computer screen, is a little bit wrong.

And yet you know exactly what a perfect circle is: every point on it is exactly the same distance from the center. Mathematicians prove things about circles that are perfectly, eternally true. So here is the puzzle. If you have never seen a perfect circle, where did you get the idea? And what are mathematicians actually talking about? Plato's answer was one of the boldest ideas in history: perfect circles really exist, but not in the world you can see and touch. They exist in a realm of unchanging, perfect realities he called the **Forms**. For the next two thousand years, Western philosophy would be, in part, a long argument about whether he was right.

sections.heading: Plato: The Student Who Wrote It All Down
sections.body:
**Plato** was born in Athens around 428 or 427 BCE into a wealthy, aristocratic family. His relatives included Critias and Charmides, two of the Thirty Tyrants we met on Day 10. As a young man he may have hoped for a political career, but two things changed his mind: the violence of the Thirty, and then the execution of his teacher Socrates by the restored democracy in 399. In a letter attributed to him (the *Seventh Letter*, whose authenticity scholars still debate), Plato says these events convinced him that no city would be well governed until philosophers ruled or rulers became philosophers. We will return to that idea on Day 14.

After traveling, including to Sicily and probably to meet Pythagoreans in southern Italy, Plato founded a school around 387 BCE in a grove outside Athens sacred to the hero Academus. It became known as the **Academy**, which is why we still call universities and scholarly life ‘academic’. It lasted, in one form or another, for centuries.

Unlike Socrates, Plato wrote, and almost all his works survive. They are **dialogues**, little dramas in which characters argue, and in most of them Socrates is the main speaker. This creates a famous puzzle. When does ‘Socrates’ speak for the historical Socrates, and when is he a mouthpiece for Plato's own ideas? Most scholars divide the dialogues roughly into an early group (like the *Apology* and *Euthyphro*), where Socrates mostly asks questions and ends in puzzlement, a middle group (like the *Phaedo*, *Republic* and *Symposium*), where Socrates confidently presents big theories, and a late group (like the *Parmenides*, *Sophist* and *Laws*). The Theory of Forms belongs mainly to the middle period. It is usually treated as Plato's own idea, not Socrates'. Aristotle, who studied with Plato for twenty years, says exactly this: Socrates searched for definitions, but did not make them exist separately; Plato did.

sections.heading: From Socrates' Question to Plato's Answer
sections.body:
Remember Socrates' favorite question from Day 9: What is courage? What is justice? What is piety? In the *Euthyphro*, Socrates tells Euthyphro he does not want a list of pious actions. He wants the one thing, the single form or character, that makes all pious actions pious. Give me that, he says, and I can use it as a model, a standard, to judge any action.

Plato took this demand seriously and asked: what kind of thing could that standard be? It cannot be any particular action, because any particular pious act is pious in one way and perhaps impious in another. It cannot be a physical object, because physical objects change. And it cannot just be an idea in someone's head, because then justice would be different for each person, which is exactly the relativism of Protagoras that we saw on Day 8.

So Plato concluded that there must exist something objective, unchanging and perfect: **Justice itself**, **Beauty itself**, **Equality itself**. He called these the **Forms** (in Greek, *eidos* or *idea*). The many things we see around us, such as this just law, that beautiful sunset, these two equal sticks, are **particulars**. They are just, beautiful or equal only because they **participate** in, or imitate, the corresponding Form.

Here is the key contrast:

- Forms are **eternal**; particulars come into being and pass away.
- Forms are **unchanging**; particulars are constantly changing.
- Forms are **perfect**; particulars are imperfect copies.
- Forms are **known by reason**; particulars are perceived by the senses.
- A Form is **one**; particulars are many.

Notice that the Forms are not ‘ideas’ in the modern sense of thoughts in a mind, even though the Greek word *idea* gave us the English word. A Form would exist even if no one ever thought about it, just as the truths of geometry are true whether or not anyone has discovered them.

sections.heading: Two Worlds: Uniting Heraclitus and Parmenides
sections.body:
Plato's theory brilliantly combines two thinkers you have already met. Heraclitus (Day 4) said everything flows; you cannot step into the same river twice. Parmenides (Day 5) said that true being cannot change, and that only reason, not the senses, can grasp it. These look like opposite views. Plato's genius was to say: both are right, but about different things.

Aristotle tells us that in his youth Plato became familiar with the ideas of Cratylus, a follower of Heraclitus, and came to believe that the sensible world is in constant flux and cannot be the object of true knowledge. From Socrates he took the search for stable definitions. Put them together and you get what is often called Plato's **two worlds** picture:

1. The **world of becoming**: the physical world we perceive with our senses. Here Heraclitus is right. Everything changes, and our beliefs about it are at best opinion.
2. The **world of being**: the realm of the Forms. Here Parmenides is right. What truly is does not change, and it can be known with certainty by reason.

In the *Phaedo*, Plato gives a clear argument using equality. Consider two sticks that look equal. Yet, he observes, the same sticks can seem equal to one person and unequal to another, or equal in one respect and unequal in another. But **Equality itself** never seems unequal. So Equality itself is not the same thing as equal sticks. And since we judge that the sticks *fall short* of perfect equality, we must already know what perfect equality is. Where did we get that knowledge? Not from the sticks, which never show it to us perfectly.

The ‘two worlds’ language is a useful simplification, but scholars warn against taking it too literally. The Forms are not located in some distant place, like another planet. They are not in space or time at all. The point is that there are two very different kinds of reality, with different degrees of being and knowability, and the physical world depends on the Forms the way a reflection depends on the object it reflects. We will see Plato's most vivid picture of this on Day 12, in the Allegory of the Cave.

sections.heading: The Form of the Good
sections.body:
If there are many Forms, are some more important than others? In the *Republic*, Plato places one Form above all the rest: the **Form of the Good**. It is so exalted that Socrates in the dialogue refuses to define it directly, offering an analogy instead.

Think of the sun, he says. The sun does two things for visible objects. It gives them light, so that we can see them, and it makes them grow and live. The Form of the Good does the same for the Forms. It makes them knowable, and it is in some way the source of their very being. Plato even says, in a famously puzzling phrase, that the Good is beyond being, surpassing it in dignity and power.

Why put goodness at the top of reality? For Plato, to understand anything fully is to understand what it is good for, why it is the way it is, and why that is best. A knife's nature is defined by cutting well; an eye's by seeing well. Ultimately, he believed, the whole structure of reality is ordered by goodness, so the deepest knowledge of the world and the deepest knowledge of how to live turn out to be the same thing. This is why, on Day 14, Plato will argue that only those who have grasped the Good should rule.

Many readers find the Form of the Good mysterious, and with reason. Plato never gives a complete account, and his students apparently found it puzzling too. An ancient report says that when Plato gave a public lecture *On the Good*, the audience came expecting advice on wealth and happiness and were bewildered to hear mostly about mathematics, ending with the claim that the Good is One. Later, the Neoplatonist Plotinus (Day 28) would build an entire philosophy on identifying the Good with the One.

sections.heading: Recollection: The Slave Boy in the Meno
sections.body:
If the Forms are not in the physical world, how do we come to know them? Plato's answer is the theory of **recollection** (*anamnesis*): learning is really remembering.

The idea is introduced in the *Meno* through a puzzle known as **Meno's paradox**. How can you search for something you do not know? If you already know it, you do not need to search. If you do not know it, you will not recognize it when you find it. So inquiry seems impossible.

Socrates responds by calling over an uneducated slave boy belonging to Meno and drawing a square in the sand, two feet on each side, so four square feet in area. How long must the side be, he asks, to make a square of double the area, eight square feet? The boy confidently says: double the side, four feet. Socrates draws it. That square has an area of sixteen, four times too big. The boy tries three feet; that gives nine, still wrong. Now he is confused, and Socrates points out that this is progress: he no longer falsely thinks he knows. Then, by asking only questions, Socrates leads him to see that the square built on the **diagonal** of the original square has exactly double the area.

Socrates claims he has taught the boy nothing, only asked questions. So where did the knowledge come from? It must already have been in him. Plato concludes that the soul existed before birth, knew the truth, and forgot it at birth. Learning is the process of recollecting, triggered by questioning or by imperfect copies in the world, like the equal sticks.

Critics have pointed out that Socrates' questions are very leading, and that the boy is drawing on his ability to follow reasoning, not on memories from a previous life. Many modern philosophers would say the episode shows that some knowledge is **a priori**, known by reason rather than experience, without proving reincarnation. That debate, about whether some knowledge is innate, will flare up again with Descartes (Day 43) and Locke's attack on innate ideas (Day 47).

sections.heading: Problems with the Forms: The Third Man
sections.body:
One of the most remarkable things about Plato is that he criticized his own theory. In the late dialogue *Parmenides*, the young Socrates explains the Forms to the aged Parmenides, who proceeds to tear them apart.

First, Parmenides asks which things have Forms. Justice, Beauty and Goodness, certainly. What about human being, fire or water? Socrates is unsure. And what about hair, mud and dirt? Socrates thinks it would be absurd to posit a Form of Mud, but worries that he cannot say why some things get Forms and others do not.

Second comes the most famous objection, which Aristotle later named the **Third Man** argument. Here it is with large things:

1. Many particular things are large. We explain this by saying they all share in one Form, Largeness itself.
2. But on Plato's view, Largeness itself is also large; indeed, perfectly large. (This assumption that a Form has the property it explains is called **self-predication**.)
3. Now put Largeness itself alongside the large particulars. They all have something in common: they are all large. So by the same reasoning as in step 1, there must be a further Form, a second Largeness, that explains what they share.
4. But then that second Form is large too, so we need a third, and so on forever.

The theory seemed to promise one Form for each kind of thing, but it generates an **infinite regress**, an endless chain of Forms. Aristotle's version used man: if a man and the Form of Man share something, there must be a ‘third man’ above both.

How did Plato respond? Scholars disagree sharply. Some think he abandoned or heavily revised the theory in his later years. Others think he was showing that self-predication must be understood differently: Largeness is not large the way an elephant is large; it is what largeness *is*. Still others think he included the objections as an exercise for his students.

Aristotle, Plato's greatest pupil, was not satisfied with any of these answers. He would argue that Forms do not exist separately at all, but only *in* things. We will follow that argument on Day 16.

keyQuote.text: The safest general characterization of the European philosophical tradition is that it consists of a series of footnotes to Plato.
keyQuote.source: Alfred North Whitehead, Process and Reality (1929)

modernConnection.title: Do Numbers Exist? Platonism in Mathematics and Machine Learning
modernConnection.body:
Plato's Forms may sound like ancient mysticism, but the question behind them is alive in modern mathematics. Is the number 7 something mathematicians *discover*, or something humans *invent*? Many working mathematicians feel like explorers. The mathematician G. H. Hardy wrote that mathematical reality lies outside us and that our job is to discover or observe it. Kurt Gödel, the great twentieth-century logician, defended a version of this view, often called **mathematical Platonism**: numbers and sets are real, abstract, non-physical objects that we grasp by a kind of intellectual perception. Their opponents, such as formalists and fictionalists, argue that mathematics is more like an elaborate, extremely useful game or story we have created.

There is a striking modern twist on Plato's question from artificial intelligence. When an image-recognition system learns to identify cats, it is shown many thousands of particular cats, all different: fat, thin, ginger, black, sleeping, jumping. Eventually it can recognize cats it has never seen before. Has it grasped the ‘Form of Cat’? Not in Plato's sense. What it has learned is a complex statistical pattern built entirely from particulars, which is closer to Aristotle's view (Day 16) that we abstract general concepts from experience. And the system can be fooled by small changes that no human would notice, a reminder that it has learned something quite different from a definition.

In fact, machine learning suggests a challenge to Plato. Perhaps many of our concepts, like ‘game’ or ‘chair’, have no single essence at all, only overlapping similarities. Wittgenstein will make exactly this argument with his idea of **family resemblance** on Day 73. Yet mathematics remains the hardest case for anti-Platonists: a perfect circle still cannot be found in any dataset, and the theorems about it are still true.

vocabulary.definition: In Plato, an eternal, unchanging, perfect, non-physical reality (such as Beauty itself or Equality itself) that particular things imitate or participate in, and that is known by reason.
vocabulary.example: For Plato, a just law is just only because it participates in the Form of Justice.

vocabulary.definition: An individual, concrete thing in the physical world, such as this horse or that painting, which is changing and imperfect.
vocabulary.example: Every particular circle drawn on a whiteboard falls short of the perfect circle that geometry describes.

vocabulary.definition: Plato's term for the relationship between a particular and a Form, by which the particular has the quality the Form represents.
vocabulary.example: A rose is beautiful by participation in Beauty itself, according to Plato.

vocabulary.definition: The highest Form in Plato's *Republic*, compared to the sun, which makes the other Forms knowable and is the source of their being.
vocabulary.example: Plato believed that a ruler who had grasped the Form of the Good would know what is truly best for the city.

vocabulary.definition: Plato's theory that learning is remembering knowledge the soul possessed before birth.
vocabulary.example: When the slave boy in the *Meno* realizes the answer about the diagonal, Socrates calls it recollection.

vocabulary.definition: Knowledge that can be gained by reason alone, independently of sensory experience.
vocabulary.example: That a square built on the diagonal has double the area can be known a priori, by reasoning, without measuring any squares.

vocabulary.definition: A series of explanations or steps that never ends, because each step requires another; often a sign that a theory has gone wrong.
vocabulary.example: The Third Man argument claims that the theory of Forms leads to an infinite regress of Forms of Largeness.

vocabulary.definition: The assumption that a Form has the very property it explains, for example that Largeness itself is large.
vocabulary.example: The Third Man objection depends on self-predication: if Beauty itself is beautiful, it seems to need a further Form to explain its beauty.

thinkingExercise.title: Hunting for Forms
thinkingExercise.prompt: Test Plato's theory against your own experience by looking for things that seem to need a Form, and things that seem not to.
steps: Write down three things you know about perfectly but have never seen perfectly: for example, a straight line, perfect fairness, the number 3. How did you come to know them?
Now write down three ordinary kinds of things, like 'chair', 'sandwich' or 'mud'. Do they need a Form? Try to give a definition of one of them that covers all cases.
Choose a value word, like 'justice' or 'beauty'. If there is no Form of it, what makes one act more just than another? Write down the best alternative answer you can think of.
Explain the Third Man argument in your own words to an imaginary friend in three or four sentences. Then write down one way a defender of Plato might reply.

summary: Plato (c. 428/427–348/347 BCE), Socrates' student and founder of the Academy, wrote dialogues in which the Theory of Forms appears mainly in the middle period.
Forms are eternal, unchanging, perfect, non-physical realities known by reason; particulars are changing, imperfect copies known by the senses.
The 'two worlds' picture combines Heraclitus (the sensible world flows) with Parmenides (true being is unchanging and known by reason).
The Form of the Good, compared to the sun, is the highest Form, the source of the knowability and being of the others.
In the *Meno*, the slave-boy episode supports the theory of recollection: learning is remembering what the soul knew before birth.
Plato himself raised serious problems, especially the Third Man regress, which Aristotle would use to reject separate Forms.

quiz.question: Which of the following best describes a Platonic Form?
options: A thought or concept in the mind of an individual person
A perfect, eternal, unchanging reality known by reason
The physical shape of an object
An average of all the particular examples we have seen
quiz.explanation: Forms are objective, perfect and eternal, grasped by reason. They are not mental ideas, physical shapes or statistical averages.

quiz.question: How does Plato's 'two worlds' picture combine earlier thinkers?
options: It agrees with the Atomists that only atoms and void exist
It follows Protagoras in making each person the measure of truth
It makes Heraclitus right about the sensible world and Parmenides right about true being
It follows Thales in making water the first principle
quiz.explanation: The sensible world flows, as Heraclitus said, while the realm of Forms is unchanging and knowable by reason, as Parmenides insisted.

quiz.question: According to Aristotle, the theory of separately existing Forms was Plato's development rather than the historical Socrates' own view.
quiz.explanation: Aristotle says Socrates sought universal definitions but did not make them exist separately; Plato did.

quiz.question: In the *Meno*, what does Socrates claim the slave-boy episode demonstrates?
options: That slaves cannot learn geometry
That knowledge comes only from sense experience
That learning is recollection of what the soul already knew
That doubling the side of a square doubles its area
quiz.explanation: Socrates says he taught nothing and only asked questions, so the knowledge must have been in the boy already. Doubling the side actually quadruples the area, which was the boy's mistake.

quiz.question: What problem does Meno's paradox raise?
options: How we can search for something we do not know, since we would not recognize it if we found it
Whether virtue can be bought and sold
Why mathematical objects change over time
How the soul can be divided into three parts
quiz.explanation: The paradox claims inquiry is either unnecessary (if we know) or impossible (if we don't). Recollection is Plato's answer.

quiz.question: In the *Republic*, what is the Form of the Good compared to?
options: A river
A ladder
A ship
The sun
quiz.explanation: Like the sun, which gives visibility and growth to visible things, the Good gives knowability and being to the Forms.

quiz.question: In the *Parmenides*, Plato presents only arguments in favor of the Forms and none against them.
quiz.explanation: The *Parmenides* contains powerful objections to the Forms, including the regress later called the Third Man.

quiz.question: Which assumption is the Third Man argument most dependent on?
options: That the soul existed before birth
Self-predication: that a Form has the property it explains
That the senses are always reliable
That there is a Form of mud
quiz.explanation: If Largeness itself is large, it shares largeness with large things, and a new Form seems needed to explain what they share, generating a regress.

quiz.question: Which modern position is closest to Plato's view of the Forms?
options: The view that mathematics is a useful game humans invented
Mathematical Platonism, which holds that numbers are real abstract objects we discover
The view that concepts are just patterns learned from data
The view that each person decides what is true for them
quiz.explanation: Mathematical Platonists like Gödel held that numbers and sets exist independently of us. The other options are anti-Platonist or relativist.

quiz.question: For Plato, two sticks that look equal are themselves a perfect example of Equality.
quiz.explanation: In the *Phaedo*, the sticks fall short of Equality itself; they may seem equal in one way and unequal in another, while Equality itself never seems unequal.

goDeeper.body:
The Third Man argument became a battleground of twentieth-century scholarship. In 1954, Gregory Vlastos published a famous paper arguing that the regress depends on two hidden assumptions that Plato held but could not consistently combine: self-predication (the Form of F is itself F) and non-identity (whatever is F is not identical with the Form by which it is F). If you hold both, Vlastos argued, the regress is unavoidable, and Plato never clearly saw this. His paper launched decades of debate. Some, like G. E. L. Owen, argued that Plato did see the problem and revised his theory in late works like the *Sophist* and *Timaeus*. Others proposed that statements like 'Beauty is beautiful' should be read differently from 'Helen is beautiful': not as describing a feature Beauty has, but as stating what Beauty is.

A second debate concerns how many worlds Plato really believed in. The 'two worlds' interpretation, popular in textbooks, suggests the Forms and particulars are two separate realms with two separate kinds of mental state: knowledge for Forms, opinion for particulars. Gail Fine has argued for a 'one world' reading, on which knowledge and opinion can be about the same things, and the difference lies in whether one can give an explanation grounded in the Forms. This matters because the two-worlds view seems to imply that we can never have knowledge about the physical world at all, a conclusion modern science finds hard to accept.

Finally, Plato's late dialogue *Timaeus* offers a creation story in which a divine craftsman, the Demiurge, shapes the physical world by looking to the Forms as a model, building the elements from mathematical triangles. This dialogue, widely available in Latin translation, was the most influential Platonic text in the early Middle Ages.

readings.note: Short and very readable. Focus on the slave-boy episode (roughly 82b–86c in standard numbering).

readings.title: Phaedo
readings.author: Plato
readings.note: Read the argument about equal sticks and Equality itself (roughly 74a–76e).

readings.author: Julia Annas
readings.note: A clear, opinionated guide by a leading scholar, with a good chapter on the Forms.

readings.author: Plato (trans. Mary Louise Gill and Paul Ryan)
readings.note: For the ambitious: read the first part (to about 135c), where Parmenides attacks the Forms.

questions: If the Forms do not exist, what makes mathematical statements true? Are you more comfortable saying humans invented mathematics or discovered it?
Is it a strength or a weakness that Plato criticized his own most famous theory?
Can a value like justice be objective without being a separately existing Form?
